## Framing

Many things can influence a child's opportunities to learn spoken words. Given those opportunities, many further factors can affect how well a child learns new words and how easily they can say them. These include biological, social and educational factors, and their interactions. While age does not *directly* influence the number of words a child says, it does influence essentially all of those factors and therefore *indirectly* influences spoken word learning. In this study our goal is to estimate trajectories of word learning over time. We are not trying to disentangle the specific causal effects of different factors on word learning, but rather to capture the overall age-associated change in spoken vocabulary.

The overall interaction of age with spoken word learning is therefore complex and likely to be nonlinear. Children may learn words more quickly at some ages than others [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994], and there may be periods of plateau.

Both experience and existing research indicate substantial variability in vocabulary development among children with Down syndrome [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994; @berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008; @kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013; @deckersPredictorsReceptiveExpressive2019], and developmental trajectories more generally [@karmiloff-smithImportanceUnderstandingIndividual2016; @fidlerExploratoryBehaviorDevelopmental2019; @thedownsyndromecognitionprojectCapturingCognitiveBehavioral2021]. This variability appears to grow over time as children making more progress diverge from those making less progress. We therefore expect the variance in spoken word learning to increase with age, but not to increase indefinitely — and the Beta-Binomial dispersion structure described in the [methods chapter](methods.qmd) is designed to express precisely that.

### Causal diagram

In this model (@fig-vg01-dag), $A$ represents age and $S$ represents words spoken. $O$ represents other (unmeasured) factors that influence spoken word learning and are themselves influenced by age — word meanings already learned, opportunities to hear spoken words, explicit teaching and therapy.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-vg01-dag
//| fig-cap: "**A simple model of spoken word learning**. $A$: age; $O$: other unmeasured factors; $S$: words spoken."
//| fig-width: 2.5
//| fig-height: 0.85
digraph SimpleDAG {
    graph [size="2.5,0.85", ratio=fill, rankdir=LR]
    edge [arrowsize=0.75]
    node [shape=square]
    O [shape=circle]

    A -> O
    O -> S
}
```

The causal effect of $A$ on $S$ is entirely mediated through $O$, and since $A$ is exogenous there are no open backdoor paths from age to spoken vocabulary. Conditioning on age suffices to identify the total age-associated change in words spoken.

## Model specification

VG01 instantiates the shared model backbone described in the [methods chapter](methods.qmd) with `n_trials = 800`, slope anchors $(24, 84)$ months, and the model-specific slope-anchor priors below.

### Slope-anchor priors

Previous research and professional experience suggest that many children with Down syndrome are saying very few spoken words at 24 months, but we allow substantial uncertainty up to ~100 words:

$$p_{24} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1, 15).$$

![Prior distribution for the lower slope anchor (spoken words at 24 months)](figures/VG01-age-spoken-ds/p_slope_low_dist.png){#fig-vg01-slope-low width="5in"}

At 84 months a wide range of ability is expected. We are less confident about the distribution but suspect some children may still be saying few words, while others will be saying close to 800. We specify $p_{84} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(1.1, 1.1)$, which is approximately uniform:

![Prior distribution for the upper slope anchor (spoken words at 84 months)](figures/VG01-age-spoken-ds/p_slope_hi_dist.png){#fig-vg01-slope-hi width="5in"}

The remaining priors ($\ell$, $\eta$, $\kappa_{\min}$, $a_\kappa$, $b_{\text{mag}}$) follow the family-wide values in the [methods chapter](methods.qmd).

## Results

### Diagnostics

VG01 sampled at rep quality (6 chains × 6 000 + 6 000 NUTS, target_accept = 0.95): r̂_max = 1.001, ESS_bulk_min = 11 518 across reported parameters (ESS_bulk_max = 43 667), zero divergences, 12 m 31 s wall time. elpd_loo = −4 761.6 (n = 949 observations); all Pareto $\hat k$ values within the reliable range.

### Population trajectory

The full posterior summary table, the prior- and posterior-predictive figures, the smoothed median trend and the age-varying dispersion plots are in `output/models/VG01-age-spoken-ds/`. The rendered per-model report is `output/models/VG01-age-spoken-ds/index.html`.

The VG01 spoken trajectory tracks the marginal spoken trajectories of VG05–VG09 (the DS joint models) reasonably closely at the population level, with the differences attributable to the structural choices in the joint family (production-ratio reparameterisation, study REs in VG07, subject REs in VG08/VG09). VG01 is the model to consult when the question is purely about words spoken without conditioning on words understood; VG09 is the model to consult when the production–comprehension relationship is in scope.

## Status of VG01 in the family

VG01 is the canonical reference model for the modelling backbone. It is the model whose posterior is most fully reported in the per-model output catalogue (it predates the bivariate machinery) and is the easiest target for prior- and posterior-predictive sanity checks. It does not include study or subject random intercepts; the corresponding pooled analysis is therefore subject to the same compositional artefacts identified for VG02 and VG05 in the [model comparison chapter](model-comparison.qmd), but the effect is smaller for the spoken outcome than for the understood outcome.

## Limitations

- **Representativeness of the sample.** The pooled DS dataset is drawn from ten studies of varying recruitment strategies. Families experiencing additional difficulties may be under-represented (declining to participate, or not being approached); families with children making strong progress may also be under-represented if they perceive less need for research participation. The model cannot correct for selection bias in the underlying samples.
- **Univariate framing.** VG01 ignores the relationship between words understood and words spoken. For DS this relationship is the most important developmental signal in the data and is therefore the focus of the joint models VG05–VG09.
- **Pooled study composition.** The model treats every observation as an exchangeable draw, with no study or subject random intercepts. The same compositional shifts that affect VG02 and VG05 (Studies 1, 2, 6, 7 contributing understood data only up to ~50 months) also affect VG01 to a lesser degree; an analogous study-RE version of VG01 has not been fitted but would be worth considering for consistency.
